# Book I, Proposition 23

*An angle equal to a given one, on a given straight line*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> On a given straight line and at a point on it to construct a rectilineal angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument · one of our tacit rules already contains it (see Overlap)

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/23-idea.svg" alt="To copy an angle (yellow) at a point on a straight line, copy a triangle about it with the same three sides (red, blue and black), and the angle comes with it." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>To copy an angle (yellow) at a point on a straight line, copy a triangle about it with the same three sides (red, blue and black), and the angle comes with it.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/23.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.23, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let AB be the given straight line, A the point on it, and the angle DCE the given rectilineal angle;

thus it is required to construct on the given straight line AB, and at the point A on it, a rectilineal angle equal to the given rectilineal angle DCE.

On the straight lines CD, CE respectively let the points D, E be taken at random;

let DE be joined,

and out of three straight lines which are equal to the three straight lines CD, DE, CE let the triangle AFG be constructed in such a way that CD is equal to AF, CE to AG, and further DE to FG. [I. 22]

Then, since the two sides DC, CE are equal to the two sides FA, AG respectively,

and the base DE is equal to the base FG,

the angle DCE is equal to the angle FAG. [I. 8]

Therefore on the given straight line AB, and at the point A on it, the rectilineal angle FAG has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal angle DCE.

Q. E. F.

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop23.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop23.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where the statement already gives a step; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Already given.** "thus it is required to construct on the given straight line AB…" The statement gives the task: an angle FAG equal to the angle DCE, with G on the ray from A through B and F on P's side of AB.
- **Already given.** "On the straight lines CD, CE respectively let the points D, E be taken at random…" The statement names a point on each arm, D on CD and E on CE, and we take those; any others would serve, for an angle depends only on its two rays.
- **Already given.** "let DE be joined…" Our triangle DCE is named by its corners, so no straight line DE is drawn; its three sides are the three straight lines that I.22 takes.

```lean
/-- On a given straight line and at a point on it to construct a rectilineal angle equal to a given
rectilineal angle. -/
theorem Prop23 {A B C D E P : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hDCE : Triangle D C E) (hP : ¬ Collinear A B P) :
    ∃ F G : Point, OnRay G A B ∧ SameSideOf F P A B ∧ ∠ F A G = ∠ D C E := by
  -- Let AB be the given straight line, A the point on it, and the angle DCE the given
  -- rectilineal angle;
  /- The given angle comes as the triangle DCE: its arms CD, CE are two straight
     lines through C, not one, so it is a true rectilineal angle. We shall need the
     straight line AB itself, to see that the angle we build is not flat either. -/
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  -- thus it is required to construct on the given straight line AB, and at the point A on it,
  -- a rectilineal angle equal to the given rectilineal angle DCE.
  /- We build the angle on the ray from A through B, and on the side of AB where P
     is, so that later propositions can place it where they need it (I.24, I.31). -/
  -- On the straight lines CD, CE respectively let the points D, E be taken at random;
  /- The statement already names a point on each arm, D on CD and E on CE, so we
     take those. Any others would do as well: an angle depends only on its two rays
     (`angle_eq_of_onRay` in Book Zero). -/
  -- let DE be joined,
  /- Our proof uses only the points D and E; the straight line DE is drawn for the eye.
     Joined, it closes the triangle DCE, whose three sides are the three straight
     lines that I.22 is about to take. -/
  -- and out of three straight lines which are equal to the three straight lines CD, DE, CE let
  -- the triangle AFG be constructed in such a way that CD is equal to AF, CE to AG, and
  -- further DE to FG. [I. 22]
  /- I.22 asks that two of the three taken together in any manner be greater than the
     remaining one, and points to I.20 for it. The three are the sides of the
     triangle DCE, so I.20, applied to it named from C, says just that, once each sum
     is read in I.22's order. -/
  obtain ⟨hDE_lt, hCE_lt, hCD_lt⟩ := Prop20 hDCE.bac
  have h₁ : ‖D E‖ < ‖C D‖ + ‖C E‖ := by
    rw [← len_symm D C]
    exact hDE_lt
  have h₂ : ‖C E‖ < ‖C D‖ + ‖D E‖ := hCE_lt
  have h₃ : ‖C D‖ < ‖C E‖ + ‖D E‖ := by
    rw [add_comm, len_symm C E]
    exact hCD_lt
  /- I.22 puts the corner of its triangle at A, the side AG along the ray from A
     through B, and the third corner F on P's side of AB. Its lengths, in its own
     order and Euclid's, are CD, CE and DE. Heath notes that Euclid asks more of
     I.22 here than I.22, as Euclid gives it, provides: a triangle placed on a given
     straight line at a given point (vol. 1, p. 295). Our I.22 is stated so as to
     provide it. -/
  obtain ⟨G, F, hG, hF, hFA_CD, hAG_CE, hGF_DE⟩ :=
    Prop22 (A₁ := C) (A₂ := D) (B₁ := C) (B₂ := E) (C₁ := D) (C₂ := E) h₁ h₂ h₃ hAB hP
  /- Euclid calls AFG a triangle, and I.8 will need it to be one. G is on the
     straight line AB (a point of the ray from A through B, so not A itself), and F,
     being on one side of AB, is off it (`OnRay.onLine`, `SameSideOf.triangle`,
     `Triangle.off_line`, `Triangle.of_line` in Book Zero). -/
  have hG_AB : OnLine G AB := hG.onLine hA_AB hB_AB
  have hA_G : A ≠ G := hG.2.1.symm
  have hF_AB : ¬ OnLine F AB := hF.triangle.off_line hA_AB hB_AB
  have hAFG : Triangle A F G := (Triangle.of_line hA_AB hG_AB hA_G hF_AB).acb
  -- Then, since the two sides DC, CE are equal to the two sides FA, AG respectively,
  have hCD_AF : ‖C D‖ = ‖A F‖ := hFA_CD.symm.trans (len_symm F A)
  have hCE_AG : ‖C E‖ = ‖A G‖ := hAG_CE.symm
  -- and the base DE is equal to the base FG,
  have hDE_FG : ‖D E‖ = ‖F G‖ := hGF_DE.symm.trans (len_symm G F)
  -- the angle DCE is equal to the angle FAG. [I. 8]
  have hDCE_FAG : ∠ D C E = ∠ F A G := Prop8 hDCE.bac hAFG hCD_AF hCE_AG hDE_FG
  -- Therefore on the given straight line AB, and at the point A on it, the rectilineal angle
  -- FAG has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal angle DCE.
  exact ⟨F, G, hG, hF, hDCE_FAG.symm⟩
  -- Q. E. F.
```

- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)

- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_of_on_inside_outside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L195): Two circles cut one another if the first passes through a point A inside the second, and a point B outside the second is inside or on the first. (Intersection 4, in LeanEuclid's corrected form)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)

- [`inside_not_on`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L38): A point inside a circle is not on it. (Generalities 4)
- [`inside_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L161): A circle is "convex": between two points on or inside it, every point is inside. (Circle 2)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, heading out to a point C outside it, cuts the circle between B and C. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, produced beyond B away from C, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)

- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L179): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L. (Intersection 1)

- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L49): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L52): If B is between A and C, then A is not between B and C. (Between 1)

- [`on_line_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L61): A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them. (Between 3)

- [`pasch3`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L114): A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3)

If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26) (used here): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**Oenopides' angle.** An angle is hard to carry about, but a triangle is only three lengths, which I.22 can set down anywhere: so Euclid copies the triangle DCE at A, and I.8 brings the angle with it. Heath writes: "This problem was, according to Eudemus (see Proclus, p. 333, 5), 'rather the discovery of Oenopides,' from which we must apparently infer, not that Oenopides was the first to find any solution of it, but that it was he who discovered the particular solution given by Euclid" (vol. 1, p. 295).

**"Not exactly the construction given in I. 22."** The editors, Heath notes, seem to have missed it: "We have here to construct a triangle on a certain finite straight line AG as base; in I. 22 we have only to construct a triangle with sides of given length without any restriction as to how it is to be placed" (vol. 1, p. 295). He suspects Proclus felt it too, and so gave the construction over again "in a more instructive manner" (vol. 1, p. 295). Our I.22 is stated to close the gap.

**Apollonius' short cut.** Proclus objects to Apollonius' way, which leans on Book III: circles of one radius about the vertex and about A, equal circumferences cut off on them, and the angles equal as standing on equal circumferences. As under I.11, Heath reads him kindly: "It seems to me probable that his construction was only given from the point of view of *practical*, not theoretical, geometry" (vol. 1, p. 296). Done with compasses, by the chord, it is Euclid's construction with an isosceles triangle: the way an angle is copied to this day.

**Which side, and which way?** Euclid's "on the given straight line AB" leaves open which way along it the angle opens, and on which side, and I.24, I.31 and I.42 will care. So our statement settles both as Heath's figure does: G on the ray from A through B, F on the side of AB where a given point P lies. D and E, "taken at random", may be any points of the arms, since an angle depends only on its rays. Nor does Euclid check I.22's condition: the three lengths are the sides of the triangle DCE, and I.20 grants it.

**The modern way.** In the complex plane, multiplying by w turns every direction through the angle arg w. So the point A + (B − A)(E − C)/(D − C) makes with AB, at A, an angle equal to DCE, and its mirror image in the straight line AB makes the same angle on the other side; which of the two lies on P's side is a matter of one sign.

## Further reading

- For copying an angle with one multiplication, and its mirror image with one conjugation, Liang-shin Hahn's [*Complex Numbers and Geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1090/text/052) (1994), the chapter "Complex Numbers", where the book begins.
- For Euclid's figure as a real part of his proof, as here, where it settles which side and which way, Nathaniel Miller's [*Euclid and His Twentieth Century Rivals*](https://web.stanford.edu/group/cslipublications/cslipublications/site/9781575865072.shtml) (2007), ch. 3, "Diagrammatic Proofs", a short book that builds a formal system around Euclid's diagrams, complete with a computer proof checker.
